summary: Sirach 7 gathers short instructions about avoiding evil, refusing arrogance, guarding speech, praying and giving alms, valuing loyal relationships, managing a household, honoring parents, supporting priests, and caring for the poor, grieving, sick, and dead. The chapter moves from personal restraint to public and household responsibilities, ending with a call to remember eternity in all speech.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows Sirach’s wisdom as practical formation: reverence for God is expressed in ordinary decisions about ambition, money, speech, labor, family, worship, and mercy. It also exposes the book’s ancient household world, including counsel about servants, daughters, and discipline that modern readers need to read with historical distance.

context.author: Yeshua (Jesus) son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; the Greek translation was made by his unnamed grandson.
context.audience: Students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and later Greek-reading Jews in Egypt or the wider diaspora through the grandson’s translation.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC, likely around 180–175 BC; the Greek translation followed after the grandson came to Egypt, commonly understood as 132 BC.
context.setting: Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule, with temple worship and priesthood central, and Jewish scribal learning taking place in a Greek-speaking Mediterranean world.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction made of compact maxims and practical teaching.

outline.heading: Avoid evil and arrogant ambition
outline.note: The chapter opens with warnings against wrongdoing, self-justification, seeking honor, and pursuing judicial power without integrity.

outline.heading: Sin, prayer, mercy, and speech
outline.note: Public disgrace, repeated sin, presumptuous offerings, neglect of alms, mockery, lying, and empty speech are rejected.

outline.heading: Work, humility, friendship, and marriage
outline.note: The teacher commends created labor, warns about sinners and judgment, and values loyal friends and a wise wife over wealth.

outline.heading: Household power and family responsibilities
outline.note: The instructions address servants, cattle, children, daughters, marriage, wives, and repayment of honor to parents.

outline.heading: Reverence, priests, and offerings
outline.note: Fear of the Lord is paired with reverence for priests, ministers, and the portions commanded for worship.

outline.heading: Care for the poor, dead, grieving, and sick
outline.note: The chapter closes by extending generosity and presence to vulnerable people and by urging remembrance of eternity.

keyVerses.text: Do no evil, so no evil will overtake you.
keyVerses.why: This opening sentence gives the chapter its first moral frame: turn away from evil rather than assuming its consequences can be managed later.

keyVerses.text: Don’t babble in the assembly of elders. Don’t repeat your words in your prayer.
keyVerses.why: The verse joins public speech and prayer, showing that wisdom includes restraint before people and before God.

keyVerses.text: Honor your father with your whole heart, and don’t forget the birth pangs of your mother.
keyVerses.why: This anchors the family section by grounding honor for parents in gratitude for life received from them.

keyVerses.text: In all your words, remember eternity, and you will never sin.
keyVerses.why: The final verse gathers the chapter’s concern with speech and conduct under the long horizon of mortality and accountability.

questions.question: What kind of chapter is this?
questions.answer: Sirach 7 is a chain of wisdom instructions rather than a story. Most lines are direct commands or warnings, moving through personal behavior, public conduct, household management, worship, and care for people in need.

questions.question: Does the chapter say every bad thing that happens is payback for a specific evil act?
questions.answer: The first verses connect wrongdoing with consequences, using the language of evil overtaking a person and unrighteous sowing being reaped. The chapter itself does not explain every case of suffering or make a full theory of reward and punishment; it gives a wisdom warning about the danger of choosing wrong.

questions.question: What does “preeminence” mean here?
questions.answer: “Preeminence” is a high or first place of honor. In this chapter it is paired with “the seat of honor from the king,” so the warning is against seeking elevated status before religious and political authorities.

questions.question: Why warn against becoming a judge?
questions.answer: Verse 6 does not reject justice itself; it warns about seeking the role of judge when one may be unable to remove iniquities or may fear a powerful person. The concern is that authority can become a “stumbling block” to uprightness when pressure from the mighty bends judgment.

questions.question: What is wrong with expecting gifts or offerings to make God accept someone?
questions.answer: Verse 9 warns against assuming that “the multitude of my gifts” or an offering to the Most High God guarantees acceptance. In the flow of the chapter, religious gifts do not cancel the need to avoid sin, pray faithfully, give alms, and speak truthfully.

questions.question: How should readers handle the verses about servants and liberty?
questions.answer: The chapter assumes an ancient household world in which servants and hirelings exist. It tells the hearer not to abuse or defraud a faithful worker, and it says to love a wise servant; that is humane counsel inside an unequal system, not a modern endorsement of slavery or coercive labor.

questions.question: Why does the chapter speak differently about sons and daughters?
questions.answer: Verses 23-25 reflect an ancient patriarchal household setting where a father is addressed as manager of children’s discipline and daughters’ marriages. Readers differ about how to receive such counsel today: some emphasize the historical household context, while others also evaluate it against broader ethical concerns about dignity, agency, and unequal power.

questions.question: What role do priests and offerings have in this chapter?
questions.answer: Verses 29-31 connect fear of the Lord with revering priests and giving the priest his commanded portion. The chapter presents worship as part of wise life, but it does so from within Jerusalem’s temple-centered world of the early second century BC.

questions.question: What does “remember eternity” mean at the end?
questions.answer: The chapter does not define the phrase in detail, but it places it after commands to help the poor, honor the dead, mourn with mourners, and visit the sick. The final line asks the reader to speak and act with the long horizon of mortality and accountability in view.

glossary.def: A farming image for wrongdoing: what a person sows is pictured as something that can later be reaped.
A place of superiority or high status, which the verse warns not to seek from the Lord.
Giving for the needy; in this chapter it is paired with prayer as a practice not to neglect.
A place associated here with gold, used to say that a true brother is not worth trading away for wealth.
Offerings mentioned as part of the priest’s commanded portion.
The final word-picture for the long horizon a person should remember in all speech.
